column2: Talaka, Agnimukha and Nalahrada, danavas, dwell there having made their homes, and likewise Prahladavarchas.
Then the netherworld named Vitala, its ground white; the two nagas Kambala and Ashvatara stand there together.
The dwelling of the great-souled Mahajambha, Hayagriva and the others, lords of the asuras, is arranged there.
From it, the ground is black, called Patalatala, the home of Shankukarna, Mahanada and Namuchi.
Above the seventh netherworld stands the earth with seven continents, joined with seven oceans and adorned with mountains.
Jambudvipa is in the middle, and beyond it Plakshadvipa;
beyond that Kraunchadvipa, and outside it Shakadvipa; beyond is Pushkaradvipa, declared the seventh.
The oceans of salt water, sugarcane juice, wine, ghee, curd and milk, and the seventh, of sweet water, is remembered.
The seven continents and oceans each have double the extent of the one before; the first is remembered as a lakh in extent.
Himavat, Hemakuta and Nishadha are in the south; Nila, Shveta and Shringa are remembered as north of Meru.
Meru stands in the middle of Jambudvipa, O Bharata; Malyavat is to be known in the east and Gandhamadana in the west.
These are remembered as the nine kings of mountains in Jambudvipa; in Plakshadvipa and the others seven mountains each are to be known.
In the midst of Pushkaradvipa is a ring-shaped mountain; one is remembered, all around, named Manasa.
The most fortunate one named Vindhya stands in Jambudvipa, where this goddess Narmada flows, carrying the world across.
The younger brother of the Vindhya, Sahya, is remembered in the south. The earth is shaped like a tortoise's back, golden and circular;
likewise that earth is described as minute by those who know much; its measure is declared to be ten crore yojanas.
At its edge all around is the one renowned as Lokaloka, swelling, golden, glorious, straight and circular;
half of it is established at thousands of yojanas, and it is just as wide; in its half the sun is placed;
it illumines light, and on the far side light is struck back; therefore that great mountain is called Lokaloka.
This Bhurloka, ending at Lokaloka, is declared to be frequented by gandharvas, yakshas, rakshasas and pishachas,
by men, beasts, deer, birds and reptiles, and by immovable beings of various forms — by these six kinds of beings.
Bhurloka and Bhuvarloka extend up to the orb of the sun; the Rudras dwell there always, ever with shining faces.
Above the orb of the sun is remembered the situation of Svarloka; in it are crores of celestial chariots in twenty-eight groups.
The pole star is the pivot above all the chariots; seven wind-currents, a lakh apart, are situated in this interval.
The first current from the earth is situated at the sphere of clouds; the wind named Avaha, which arranges the arrangements;
the second named Pravaha is bound to the orb of the sun; the third named Samvaha, that fine current, is established;
the fourth current, Udvaha, is situated in the sphere of the stars; then of the next two the work of carrying the chariots is indicated.
A crore of yojanas above the pole rises Maharloka; the seventh current named Parivaha is bound to the pole.
This, standing above the festival days, produces food and the rest; it is the dwelling of the great souls who have ceased from modifications.
There are twenty-eight crores of gods holding office there; coming from Janaloka to Svarloka at the direction of the lotus-born,
they stay there for a Manvantara, completing their own work, and ascending to Maharloka they then come back again.
In one day of Brahma, fourteen sets of gods in heaven, having done their work in order, dwell in Maharloka.
Janaloka rises two crores above Maharloka; there the asuras of the Sadhyas dwell ever happy.
Tapas rises four crore yojanas above Jana; there stand the lords of creatures, the sons of Brahma.
Satyaloka rises six crores above Tapoloka; there Virat abides surrounded by hosts of gods and asuras.
Vishnu's world rises twice as high above Brahma's world; above it in extent is joined the divine world.
Beyond Vishnu's world is the glorious great city of Shiva, twenty-two crores wide, situated above it,
radiant as ten thousand suns, endowed with every desire, laid out with many forests, adorned with heavenly rivers,
with divine chariots set with every jewel, gleaming like refined gold, with thousands of storeys, possessed of every splendour —
pervaded on every side by chariots as the sky by moons, crowded with hosts of apsarases, filled with all the vidyadharas,
with those full of the sounds of dance and song, endowed with immeasurable qualities, swift as thought, countless, with their retinues;
in places with lovely swing-houses with tinkling bells, with raised half-moons adorned with ornaments of bells,
with canopies of gems and pearls, with auspicious heaps of gems and jewels, with things adorned with every jewel, beautiful with strings of pearls,
with great divine lion thrones adorned with every jewel; in places filled with holy houses endowed with countless qualities,
in places filled with charming trees always in flower and fruit, with most lovely flower gardens in hundreds and thousands.
The holy best of rivers, flowing through seven kalpas, abides right there; a thousandth part of her portion is seen in Jambudvipa,
descended to the surface of the earth wishing to show grace to the worlds; and here is the full descent of the Ganga and the other rivers.
It is adorned with rivers flowing with nectar; step-wells set with gold and jewels, with crystal steps,
fragrant with white, red, dark and yellow lotuses, adorned with heavy five-coloured ones and golden ones,
widely blooming, glossy, glorious, five cubits wide, ten and twelve cubits, and twenty cubits,
with stalks like emerald and charming petals, full of blue lotuses and others, and long ponds here and there.
With divine beings with the faces of lions and tigers, with faces of elephants, horses and deer, with cow faces, goat faces, faces of monkeys and birds,
with one face, great faces, many faces or no face, one-footed, three-footed, many-footed or footless,
dwarfish, matted-haired, shaven, long-necked, pot-bellied, huge-bodied, great-nosed, great-eared or earless,
bearing forms of many shapes, adorned with many ornaments, wearing many garbs, divine, taking forms at will, mighty,
endowed with many powers, skilled in many shastras — countless other kinds of such beings dwell there.
Hunchbacked, dwarfish, tall, of fine bodies and fine faces, shaven, grotesque, low, short and tall of that kind,
pot-bellied, short-armed, bent, short-kneed, others with lion faces and with elephant and horse faces,
with short curly hair, beautiful and pleasing to look upon — fifty crores of female attendants of Shiva are there;
they sport in houses of gems and rubies, and sometimes outside. There, in the houses with doors on a hundred thousand storeys,
are many-coloured floors adorned with diamond and beryl. Thus with thousands of fair-faced women endowed with every quality,
countless, the Lord's city is filled on every side. In its midst is a great divine shrine, Sarvatobhadra,
like pure crystal, the first abode of the husband of Uma; there the blessed Soma dwells, worshipped by the lords of ganas,
by the siddhas who have reached their own station, and by Brahma, Vishnu and others. Glorious Dharma stands there in the Lord's shrine, sinless one.
Where the heroic bull is, there the cow-mothers always stand; there is the goddess Narmada, worshipped by gods and asuras.
By that water the cows and calves and all the gods are satisfied — Brahma, Vishnu, the lord of gods with Uma, sinless one,
the gods, sages, beings, ancestors and mothers. That world here is Shiva's world and the world of the Narmada too.
The qualities of Rudra's world are also those of the world of cows. Nanda, Bhadra, Subhadra, Sushila and Surabhi —
these five cow-mothers came forth from Shiva's world; the sixth is the goddess Narmada, wishing to show grace to the worlds.
All these, mothers of all the world, satisfy the whole universe always here with their own qualities, great king.
By cause, from Shiva's abode, following the Lord's will, from Omkara, for all worlds, they have resorted to this world.
Cows eat grass, roam in the forest, drink very clear water, give milk and purify the body — by them the world of the living lives.
Whence can there be sin for those whose house is adorned always with cows with young calves, as if with women themselves?
Those who remember the true Omkara and the Narmada as Shiva's own self have no return in the dreadful ocean of worldly existence.
Those who show supreme devotion by giving grass and water go to Shiva's world by the grace of those cows.
These mothers are always favourable and grant every desire; those who protect the auspicious cows go to Shiva's world.
Those who worship Shiva with devotion by good rites, with collected minds, obtain great enjoyments and go to Shiva's city.
The men who go with faith to the holy places that rest on Shiva, and especially to the Kalpaga and the mountain Amarakantaka,
sport with great enjoyments in the abodes of Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva. Milk, nectar, ghee, honey, curd and the like —
the one deluded does not see them in the Kalpaga, fortunate one. This I have told you, O king, the auspicious descent of the Reva.
By this story may the blessed Shiva himself be pleased with me.
Markandeya said: Listen, O king, I shall tell you properly, sinless one. The lotus, the bilva leaf, kusha and the water of the Narmada —
the Self-born Lord declared these the common cause of dharma. All dharmas, the Purana and the Shrutis are purified by faith;
by the dharma of his teaching men go to heaven. Whoever gives a wide red cloth stuffed with cotton, with its thread,
or one made of tiger-skin covered with new cloth, a black deerskin and a sacred thread, perfumed with holy incense,
with faith to one engaged in meditation on Shiva — as many as are the hairs of the threads of that cotton cloth,
for so many thousands of years he is honoured in Shiva's world; he rejoices in all worlds, enjoying pleasures in many ways,
and reaching the earth again becomes lord of a throne. Having given grass, bark and leaves, bedding, coverings and the like
on the ground to one who needs them, one is honoured in Shiva's world. Whoever gives food offered to Shiva to one who has seen Shiva —
vegetable, root or fruit — hear the fruit of his merit: as many as the grains of rice and the like, and the pieces of fruit,
for so many thousands of years he is honoured in Shiva's world. Having devoutly given alms with relishes to a devotee of Shiva,
fortunate one, one is honoured in Shiva's world for a lakh of years. Whoever gives a beautiful begging bowl well filled with rice and curd
to a devotee of Shiva — hear the fruit of his merit: a divine period equal to a crore of years, endowed with great enjoyments,
having stayed in Shiva's divine city, at its end he becomes lord of the earth. Having satisfied a devotee of Shiva with very cool water with sugar,
one rejoices in Shambhu's world for a lakh of years. Whoever gives a devotee of Shiva a pot with sugar, filled with water strained through cloth —
hear the fruit of his merit: obtaining a chariot like pure crystal, granting every desire,
he rejoices in Shiva's world for a crore of years. Whoever makes cups of palasha leaves or other leaves
and gives them to Shiva-yogis is as one who gives copper vessels. Whoever gives a well-made copper vessel to a Shiva-yogi
is honoured in Shiva's world for six crores of kalpas. One who carries a trident in hand, a spear and a water-pot on his back —
having fed him with care, one attains Shiva's world. Whoever feeds according to his means one who keeps Shiva's vow
sports with the best enjoyments, established in Shiva's world. The wise man who feeds a householder following the dharma of Shiva's order
is honoured in Shiva's world with abundant great enjoyments. The man who feeds with bulbs and the like one who keeps the vow of Shiva's order
obtains divine enjoyments, dwelling in the Lord's city. Having thus fed a Pashupata devotee and bowed to him,
one is honoured in Shiva's world with great enjoyments of many kinds. Whoever gives alms to one who bears the great vow
is honoured in Shiva's world with divine and splendid enjoyments. Having fed according to his means a man of restraint, observance and good conduct, devoted to Shiva,
one is honoured in Shiva's world. Those outside the yoga of knowledge, following the common dharma of the world,
who worship Shiva with devotion go to Shiva's world. Not by the fire of dried dung without eating, by the gift of milk, by fierce austerities
or by sacrifices do men go to that goal to which even a lowly devotee of Rudra goes.
As men obtain a good goal by the touch of the Reva's water, not so by sacrifices, gifts and other means, bull of the Bharatas.
Thus this world of Shiva has been told incidentally — the world of cows and the world of the Kalpaga, filled with devotees of Shiva.
Those who, calm through the yoga of knowledge, repeat the name of the supreme Shiva are freed from all sorrow and are ever happy.
Shiva's world is to be known as consisting of spheres and enclosures: the five elements, ego, sattva and Prakriti as the eighth.
Of such nagas crores are to be known by the thousands; because primal matter is all its limbs, it stands across, above and below.
Beyond Vishnu's world is the abode of the great-souled Kumara, like a clear pearl, endowed with supreme splendour;
beyond Skanda's world the abode of the goddess Uma is declared, like refined gold, endowed with every quality;
and beyond Uma's abode is Hara's abode, the highest, radiant as a crore of suns, endowed with every desire,
inhabited by all the countless ganas intent on yoga; by Hiranyagarbha, Kurma and others, by the Vasus, Rudras and suns
the Lord is always praised by those who long to come near him; by the calm, devoted to knowledge and meditation, living on alms, self-controlled,
that supreme abode, radiant as ten thousand suns, is to be attained, and by brahmins always doing its good deeds, their sins burned away.
The perfected, free of affliction, dwell in what is truth; men who serve the Narmada attain that state.
This I have told you, son of Pritha, as Shambhu indicated. The giving I have described rests on the bank of the Narmada;
for those who go to another holy place it is surpassed a thousandfold. They become all-knowing, all-pervading, pure and perfect;
those who do pure deeds are endowed with supreme lordship and become embodied or bodiless again at will.
Thus is the eternal, pure first abode of the husband of Uma, the divine abode of lord Shrikantha, upholder of the world,
the ninefold abode from which the Kalpaga came forth, with supreme eightfold lordship, eternal, undecaying and imperishable.
Men who always meditate on the deity by the yoga of meditation taught by an eternal guru become perfected and go to that state.
Those who practise the knowledge of Shiva on the bank of the Narmada, freed from desire and craving, also go to that city.
For one devoted to meditation on Shiva even for a single day, devoted to Shiva's dharma, there is no end to his dharma.
Because it is the essence among the dharmas of yoga it cannot be broken by the hammers of sin; it is to be known like diamond grains, therefore its fruit is great.
By that dharma, at the end of the body, one reaches the first abode, Shiva's abode, where a man sports with abundant enjoyments for ten thousand kalpas;
then at the end of ten thousand kalpas he reaches Kumara's abode, where he dwells happily sporting for half that time;
at its end he reaches Vishnu's world and dwells there again; at the end he goes to Brahma's world and dwells there too;
fallen from Brahma's world he dwells happily in Shiva's city; thus in order he reaches the worlds of Brahma, Vishnu and the rest.
Having thus delighted in all the worlds in order, reaching the world of men he should take refuge in Shiva and the Reva.
The gifts I have told you of elsewhere, O Bharata — all of them are praised at the mountain Amarakantaka.
By bathing in and drinking the Narmada, and by the water from cows' tails, freed from all impurity, well perfected, keeping a long vow,
that brahmin, having bathed them, went there to the bank of the Narmada; on the full moon, at full moon, at the conjunction of Rahu and Soma,
together with those excellent brahmins he should worship and remember Hari, joined with servants, sons, wife, his own people and kin,
and should offer to Krishna with a mantra, full of faith: "In shraddha, in giving, in fire offering, in marriage and in auspicious rites,
the cow-mothers always abide in Vishnu's world, of Shiva's nature; I have given these to Shiva and to the great-souled Vishnu."
Whoever thus gives them, adorned, to a brahmin for sacrifice — having offered thus, a man gains the fruit of a thousand cows,
and raising thirty generations, servants and kin from hell, establishes them in the world of Vishnu and of the great-souled Shiva.
All-knowing, perfect, pure, all-pervading lord, freed from the ocean of worldly existence, he becomes equal to Hari.
By this very rite householders may attain heaven, even without the yoga of knowledge, by giving a thousand cows.
A brahmin, a kshatriya or even a shudra, with devotion, at the meeting of the Narmada and Kapila, according to his means,
to a poor, initiated, well-adorned brahmin, at eclipses of moon and sun, at vyatipata and the solar transit,
should give at the Shadashitimukha, at the conjunction of the new moon with a Monday, on the full moon of Kartika, at the beginning of an age, or on a holy day, O Bharata.
For the ancestors sing this verse, lord of men: "May there be in our family a supremely righteous son
who, at the meeting of the Narmada and Kapila and at Kotitirtha, giver of liberation, giving cows together, will raise us from hell."
He sports in Vishnu's world for ten thousand years; therefore you too, king of kings, be a giver of a thousand cows,
by which your ancestors may always rejoice in heaven like gods. Now I shall tell you an ancient history.
Long ago there was a king, Yuvanashva, an emperor of great fame, with merit a hundred times Shakra's, devoted to protecting his subjects,
whose city Ayodhya shone like Brahma's world. At the beginning of the Krita age, devoted to all dharma,
saluting as was proper Vasishtha, his priest, equal to Brihaspati and Brahma, he said to that best of sages:
In what place should one perform sacrifice — at a holy place, a country or a temple? Vasishtha and all the sages said this:

On earth the holy place Naimisha is auspicious and made of all holy places; the horse sacrifice there is fruitful, crores of crores of times greater.
skandapuran:60:31	It was proclaimed in the Purana by Vishnu in the form of the Fish, O king, and proclaimed by the Sun to the son of Manu, his own son.
skandapuran:60:32	Of all the Puranas the Purana proclaimed by the Fish — the Vedas were lost long ago and were raised up by the Fish;
skandapuran:60:33	brahmins without the Vedas go on in the rites of sacrifice. Such is the holy place told you, Yuvanashva.
Having heard these words of his priest Vasishtha, he then commanded his ministers, righteous and truthful:
Take the implements of sacrifice and come quickly; let a proclamation be made in the kingdom by servants with staves in hand.
Then the gods were invited to the king's rite of sacrifice: Brahma, Vishnu, the lord of gods, Skanda and Vaishravana,
and Shambhu especially, saluted by gods and asuras. Ten lakh milch cows with gold and jewels,
one lakh horses, thirty thousand elephants, gems, rubies and pearls, and gold without end,
materials of many kinds, adorned foods and eatables, the materials of sacrifice and whatever else — with all this the king,
with many thousands of vehicles, with kings from many lands, with many thousands of instruments and many charming songs,
resounding heaven and earth with the great sound of Vedic recitation, entered the holy place Naimisha, where the god Maheshvara is,
where, seeing Hari, the lord, one is at once freed from sin; this is the stairway to heaven, visible like the world of the gods.
Bathing there and worshipping Hari and Hara, one attains heaven; by reciting the name of this Naimisha a man at once burns up
the dreadful sin of many births, as fire a heap of cotton. Initiated brahmins and gods came from everywhere;
he gave ten thousand to the distressed and to the god, sinless one, and the king gave a thousand ornaments, O Bharata.
Om, salutation to Shankara, and to Madhava, the excellent king, taking water and darbha in a golden vessel,
having thus made the resolve, king of kings, had the sacrificial enclosure made, ten yojanas in extent, with golden sacrificial posts.
Then the sacrifice was completed by the brahmins headed by Vasishtha; all the gods, delighted, mounted on divine vehicles,
raised the cry of victory: "No other king is equal to you." "No one is equal to me," the king thought with pride.
As he mounted his vehicle with his women and retinue and came out of the Naimisha forest, he saw a monkey.
It said: "Stop, stop! Hear my words, O king. What use is your rite of sacrifice and your act of giving to the gods,
when, your mind deluded by ego, you think 'I am the doer'? Long ago at the sacrifice of King Satyadharma at Amareshvara,
except for my face, everything of me below the throat became golden; the young ones who went there became golden in every limb,
at the meeting of the Kapila and Narmada, from the stream of the sacrificial water; by bathing, immersing, drinking and rolling in the mud,
the fourfold host of beings reached the gandharva world. In your sacrifice at the Naimisha forest I rolled about;
my body was smeared with mud and washed with water, but I got no fruit at all; your sacrifice is pointless.
You gave ten thousand cows and much wealth and grain; King Satyadharma — yet all this of yours is pointless.
By giving or by austerity the three worlds are won; the Mekala is remembered as the mother of all holy places.
This I have told you, O king, as it happened at Amareshvara. Blessings on you; I shall go; go you to Ayodhya.
I myself shall go to the Narmada, the Kalpaga of seven kalpas; having heard of your sacrifice I came to the Naimisha forest,
and I shall go without hope; my face did not become golden." Hearing the monkey's words, Yuvanashva said:
Who are you in the form of a monkey? Tell me this truly. The monkey said: "I am the son of Jabali, renowned as Kadamba;
I entered an animal birth through my own ordinary deeds. I have wandered through all the holy places in this guise, man of good vows;
there was no supreme deliverance until the excellent sacrifice of Satyadharma; my whole body became golden, except my face."
Hearing the monkey's words, the best of kings turned back, worshipped the lord of the god of gods, the Person of sacrifice, at Naimisha,
and bowing and appeasing him spoke gentle words: "At my sacrifice, by giving, austerity and observance,
a single being in monkey form proclaimed that I did not deserve peace; do as you will that his face may become golden."
The god spoke to Yuvanashva, lord of the earth: "Naimisha is the manifest holy place, radiant as a crore of suns;
on earth the holy place is Naimisha, in the atmosphere Pushkara; the mountain Amarakantaka is renowned in the three worlds.
And you have not heard, dear one, the Purana proclaimed by Skanda, where that best of rivers is mother of rivers and holy places;
by chanting her name one is freed from the bonds of worldly existence. Give up despondency; Amarakantaka is the chief of holy places.
Satyadharma will perform an excellent sacrifice there again; at the meeting of the Reva and Kapila your face will become golden there,
no doubt, best of monkeys." Bowing to Naimisha, to the first god Hara and to Hari,
he went to his own place filled with supreme joy. Hearing the word of Naimisha, the lord of Ayodhya too
entered the holy city as Shakra enters Amaravati. The monkey too went there, where Satyadharma himself was,
and bowing to the one called Satyadharma spoke these words: "At the meeting of the Reva and Kapila, at your great sacrifice,
from my rolling in the mud produced by the concluding bath, my body became golden; only my face remains.
Perform a sacrifice there again and make my face golden." The lord of the gandharvas was again freed from the monkey's birth.
When the best of monkeys had his body turned to gold there, adorned with many ornaments, to the sound of the gods' drums,
in a vehicle drawn by swans, fanned by hosts of apsarases, he went to Shankara's world by the power of this holy place.
All the beasts of prey there too bathed and went to heaven. This I have told you, son of Pritha, as it happened long ago;
by hearing and reciting it one gains the fruit of a thousand cows.
Markandeya said: Cows are incomparably pure, cows accomplish every aim; therefore by the gift of cows and devotion to Shiva one is freed.
The region in which one endowed with devotion to Shiva always lives becomes purified; how much more he with his kin!
Six thousand verses are told in the Purana on the bank of the Mekala — so said the knower of the truth of the yoga of knowledge and the yoga of dharma.
The nature of the courses of dharma and adharma has been described; the excellent story of the Narmada, joined with the stories of the holy places —
by reciting and hearing it one is freed from the bonds of worldly existence. The knowledge placed on a divine throne, perfumed with cloths and flowers —
having worshipped Hara and Vishnu, one should hear it and have it read. A glorious throne made of gold, very beautiful,
covered with golden cloth, adorned with many jewels, of silver, copper or bronze, made by a celibate,
arising from silver, adorned with jewels like a peak — or a divine throne, having performed worship with effort,
with hands perfumed with fragrance, seated on a glorious seat, in Shambhu's shrines and holy places, in the palaces of kings,
in houses, villages and cities, one should teach the supreme dharma; the listener to the recital of the Narmada is honoured in Shiva's world.
This holy place, that holy place — a man should not wander so; the Narmada alone is the supreme holy place, said the blessed Shiva.
At this holy place, best of men, shraddha should be performed according to rule: Yama is pleased by the welcome, Shatakratu by the seat,
the ancestors by the washing of the feet, Prajapati by the food; as long as the earth remains moist with the water of the brahmins' feet,
so long the ancestors drink water from lotus-leaf cups. To a learned graduate, a mendicant and a Vedic scholar,
and likewise to a paramahamsa and one who keeps Vishnu's vow — having given all household goods, one is honoured in Shiva's world.
Whoever makes a brahmin without the sacred fires into one who keeps the sacred fires — a brahmin, kshatriya or vaishya should do it with his own wealth —
half of that is fruitful for him as long as he lives, without doubt; and at the end, in Vishnu's world, he enjoys abundant pleasures.
The twice-born who performs a sacrifice duly with his own wealth, reaching the bank of the Narmada, rejoices in Brahma's world.
Having made a golden amalaka, one should give it to a brahmin; resorting to the bank of the Kalpaga, one is honoured in Vishnu's world.
One made in Shiva's presence of sesame, rice, camphor and fine foods mixed together, with saffron, cloth and grain —
whoever gives it on a festival day on the mountain on the bank of the Mekala dwells in Vishnu's worlds and in heaven, no doubt.
Whoever gives a living cow adorned with gold and jewels, a cow of ghee, a cow of jaggery and a cow of sugar —
having given these at the meeting of the Reva and Kapila, the best of men, freed from all sins, sports in Vishnu's world.
If, great king, begged food is offered there, it has no number, O king, as long as the confluence endures.
All this has been told you properly, man of good vows; now hear another, of the Vaivasvata Manvantara, best of kings.
Maitreya was the priest of the royal sage Virana; he had a temple of Vishnu built on the bank of the Narmada,
situated in the southern quarter of the city of Amaravati; by the greatness of that temple and the power of the Narmada
that best of brahmins rejoices in Vishnu's world for half an age. Hear of the holy places on the north-west of the Reva:
the forest named Meghavana, resting on the mountain of sacrifice; long ago the emperor Rantideva was there, Yudhishthira,
by whom the race of gods, asuras and men was brought to the cow; by whom the ancestors killed by cows long ago were released,
and those killed by chandalas reach the supreme goal. Death at the hands of a chandala, by water, a serpent, lightning or even a brahmin,
by elephants and beasts — the deaths of those full of sin — by offering bali to Vishnu and performing rites,
and by offering pindas at holy places, they go to the supreme goal. There was a royal sage named Dadhichi, lord of Avanti,
best of all upholders of dharma, valorous as Shakra. Long ago in the war of gods and asuras the gods were conquered by the daityas.
The daityas, thorns who slew gods and brahmins, perished through the fault of their own sins with servants, family and kin.
All the gods rejoiced, the world-guardians with Vasava; having made the earth and the moving and unmoving world free of obstacles,
they went to the Vindhya mountain where the Kalpaga flows. Knowing King Dadhichi to be capable, best of the Kurus,
the best of gods gave weapons to that king for protection: the thunderbolt, spear, noose, staff, sword, banner and mace,
and the trident — these are called the weapons of the gods. Having given them as was proper, they went joyfully to heaven.
Knowing the opinion of the Purana, Dadhichi, of true valour, afraid for fear of a curse, bowed and took them,
and by his power turned them into water and placed them within his body. Then, when time had passed, the danavas, proud of their strength,
headed by Jambha, Kumbha and Hayagriva, rose again. Knowing the strength of the danavas, the gods with Vasava were terrified;
when the time for action came, remembering the weapons, they sent Narada to Dadhichi, O Bharata.
Reaching the city of Avanti, the divine sage Narada entered the king's palace with its altars of gems and gold.
The tiger among kings rose, seeing the radiant sage, and worshipped him as was proper, seated on a golden seat.
Seeing him sitting at ease, the king said: "For what purpose have you come from the world of the gods to the world of men?"
Narada said: "A great war has arisen between the gods and the danavas; hand over the weapons so that the danavas may be destroyed,
and do the work of the gods, abiding in your vow of truth and dharma." Dadhichi said: "Hear, divine sage, the work for the good of the gods:
in a very short time the danavas will be destroyed. Those same weapons, great sage, I drank for safekeeping;
turned to water, they are in my body. Let them take them by some means; I will give them back."
Having said this, the best of kings summoned cows long ago; his flesh and the rest were eaten by the cows, all but the bones, lord of the people.
Then the host of weapons was obtained by the world-guardians as before; the city named Gonarda is renowned in the worlds.
The danavas were slain by the gods, and creation went on again. Then King Rantideva reflected there:
Men killed by cows, lightning, beasts, chandalas and serpents do not go to the world of the gods, nor are water-rites done for them.
Having grieved a long time, with his women and household, he washed those bones in the water of the Narmada and cast them in.
There is the linga Brahmeshvara near the mountain of sacrifice. Having fallen into doubt about dharma, King Rantideva
asked the tigers among sages, the brahmins headed by Vasishtha, having circled them three times as was proper, these words:

What regions, mountains and rivers are declared holy and auspicious, where, as they say, one may raise the ancestors who are in hell,
skandapuran:61:60	where the ancestral shraddha is imperishable and the ancestors reach an imperishable goal? The sages said: "Go with us to Markandeya's hermitage, O king;
he, dwelling on the bank of the Kalpaga, would know it all." Hearing that, Rantideva, as the sages advised,
went with the sages to him who dwells on the bank of the Kalpaga; the king with the brahmins bowed and worshipped him,
and rising, seated on a kusha seat, spoke. Markandeya said: "Whom does it not release, even dreadful ancestors, from the ocean of worldly existence?
Listen to my words, sages who know the self: the Reva is made of all holy places, auspicious and made of the self of all aims;
so it was declared by Shiva in the Purana proclaimed by Skanda — especially at the meeting of the Kubja and Reva, worshipped by the gods.
Those who bathe and die there go to heaven, free of rebirth; by the shraddha rite there the ancestors reach the supreme goal."
This I have told you, O king, of the meeting of the Kubja and Reva; having worshipped Maheshana there, called Bilvamraka,
freed from all sins one attains the leadership of ganas. A crore and a half of maidens attained supreme perfection there,
who had been cursed by former sages for the fault of desire, O Bharata; vidyadharas, yakshas, gandharvas and kinnaras,
dwellers in Kubera's city, cursed for that same fault — all of them attained perfection at the meeting of the Kubja and Reva.
At the conjunction of the new moon with a Monday and on the full moon of Kartika, Varanasi, Prayaga, Pushkara and Naimisha
come to bathe at the meeting of the Kubja and Reva. By hearing and reciting this one is honoured in Shiva's world.
